title: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition) · Units 71–72
description: Source-checked B2 vocabulary on negative and meaning-changing prefixes, Latin roots, derived word families and formal verb choices.
sourceNotice: Prepared from the user-supplied book for personal study. Targets follow the source teaching and exercise vocabulary; all example sentences and explanatory notes are newly written. No textbook passages or illustrations are reproduced.

audit.scope: Reviewed the complete teaching pages, prefix and root tables, language notes, exercises 71.1–71.5 and 72.1–72.5, and the relevant answer-key entries. Curated useful source and exercise targets without making separate cards for isolated affix fragments.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British IPA is supplied only where confidently supported; other IPA is deliberately omitted rather than guessed. A phonetic dictionary was not used for exhaustive external verification.
audit.languagePolicy: All content is English except Brazilian Portuguese translations in pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Compared the cards with the uploaded book and answer key; reviewed morphological meaning, spelling, lexical usage and register. Ran local JSON/schema, ID, provenance, example and audio-target checks. No live VocabLab app test or browser audio test was performed.
audit.limitations: No bundled word recordings; browser TTS, word recognition and import behaviour depend on the environment and are not verified here.

units.title: Unit 71 — Prefixes
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 148–149 (PDF pages 149–150).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Identify the correct negative prefix for common adjectives, including the in-/im-/ir-/il- spelling patterns.
Distinguish reversal of actions with un- and dis- from other prefix meanings.
Recognise common prefixes expressing opposition, size, number, time, repetition, excess and degree.
Build accurate word families and distinguish useful exercise contrasts such as overworked versus underpaid.

sectionsChecked: A: Negative adjective prefixes and non-negative in- meanings
B: Reversing verbs with un- and dis-
Language help on in- and prefix spelling

items.example: It would be unfair to blame one person for the entire failure.
items.note: Un- changes fair to its opposite.

items.example: An inexperienced driver should avoid difficult roads at first.
items.note: In- gives experienced a negative meaning.

items.example: The two designs look alike, but their internal structures are dissimilar.
items.note: Dis- means not similar; it is often followed by to.

items.example: The actor's voice sounded unnatural in the recording.
items.note: Un- expresses the opposite of natural.

items.example: The mushrooms were inedible, so we left them untouched.
items.note: In- means not; the word describes something that cannot safely or reasonably be eaten.

items.example: A disorganised filing system makes documents hard to find.
items.note: British spelling disorganised; US spelling disorganized.

items.example: His immature reaction made the disagreement worse.
items.note: In- becomes im- before m.

items.example: She grew impatient while waiting for the results.
items.note: In- becomes im- before p.

items.example: The committee regarded the decision as immoral.
items.note: Im- is the negative form before m, not a separate positive prefix.

items.example: It is impossible to complete the job without the right tools.
items.note: In- becomes im- before p.

items.example: It seems improbable that the two failures happened by chance.
items.note: Im- means not; improbable is less certain than impossible.

items.example: The motor produced an irregular clicking noise.
items.note: In- becomes ir- before r.

items.example: Leaving the door unlocked would be irresponsible.
items.note: Ir- gives responsible a negative meaning.

items.example: The archive contained several irreplaceable photographs.
items.note: Ir- means not; replaceable is the positive base.

items.example: Parking here is illegal after six in the evening.
items.note: In- becomes il- before l.

items.example: The handwritten label was almost illegible.
items.note: Il- means not; distinguish illegible from illiterate.

items.pt: analfabeto; que não sabe ler nem escrever
items.example: The programme supports adults who are illiterate.
items.note: Il- means not; it describes a person unable to read or write.

items.example: The engineer checked the internal connections before restarting the machine.
items.note: In- can mean inside rather than not.

items.example: Insert the card into the slot and wait for the light.
items.note: In- gives the sense of putting something into something else.

items.example: Her main source of income is freelance design work.
items.note: In- refers to money coming in; this is not a negative prefix.

items.section: B · Reversing verbs with un- and dis-
items.example: Please untie the rope before moving the boat.
items.note: Un- reverses the action of tie.

items.section: B · Reversing verbs with un- and dis-
items.example: The warning message disappeared after the restart.
items.note: Dis- reverses the sense of appear.

items.section: B · Reversing verbs with un- and dis-
items.example: I disagree with the proposed schedule.
items.note: Say disagree with a person or an opinion.

items.section: B · Reversing verbs with un- and dis-
items.example: Her parents disapprove of the plan.
items.note: The usual pattern is disapprove of something.

items.section: B · Reversing verbs with un- and dis-
items.example: There is no reason to disbelieve her account.
items.note: Dis- negates believe; disbelieve is a transitive verb.

items.section: B · Reversing verbs with un- and dis-
items.example: Disconnect the power supply before opening the case.
items.note: Dis- reverses connect; use disconnect something from something.

items.section: B · Reversing verbs with un- and dis-
items.example: High costs may discourage students from applying.
items.note: Often discourage someone from doing something.

items.section: B · Reversing verbs with un- and dis-
items.example: The new measurements could disprove the initial hypothesis.
items.note: Disprove means show that a claim is false, not merely disagree with it.

items.section: B · Reversing verbs with un- and dis-
items.example: Officials may disqualify competitors who break the rules.
items.note: Dis- removes a person's qualification to take part.

items.section: B · Reversing verbs with un- and dis-
items.example: Use the shortcut to undo the last change.
items.note: The past tense and past participle are undid and undone.

items.section: B · Reversing verbs with un- and dis-
items.example: Unfold the map so everyone can see the route.
items.note: Un- reverses fold; it can also mean develop gradually.

items.section: B · Reversing verbs with un- and dis-
items.example: The delivery team will unload the equipment this afternoon.
items.note: Un- reverses load.

items.section: B · Reversing verbs with un- and dis-
items.example: Use this code to unlock the door.
items.note: Un- reverses lock; it can refer to physical or digital access.

items.section: B · Reversing verbs with un- and dis-
items.example: The university will unveil its new research centre on Friday.
items.note: Literally remove a veil; often means publicly reveal something.

items.section: B · Reversing verbs with un- and dis-
items.example: The children could hardly wait to unwrap their presents.
items.note: Un- reverses wrap.

items.section: B · Reversing verbs with un- and dis-
items.example: Unzip the file before installing the application.
items.note: Used for opening a zip fastener or a compressed file.

items.example: She joined an anti-war demonstration in the city centre.
items.note: Anti- means against; this adjective is normally hyphenated.

items.example: His antisocial behaviour upset the neighbours.
items.note: Anti- indicates opposition to social behaviour or norms; context matters.

items.example: The doctor prescribed an antibiotic for the bacterial infection.
items.note: Anti- indicates action against something; antibiotics do not treat viruses.

items.example: She cleaned the small cut with an antiseptic solution.
items.note: An antiseptic helps prevent infection.

items.example: The writer signed an autograph after the talk.
items.note: Auto- means oneself; an autograph is a person's own signature.

items.example: The aircraft was flying on autopilot for part of the journey.
items.note: Auto- suggests that a system can operate automatically; the source writes auto-pilot.

items.example: Her autobiography describes her early career in detail.
items.note: Auto- means self; an autobiography is written about one's own life.

items.example: The two countries signed a bilateral agreement.
items.note: Bi- means two; bilateral involves two sides or parties.

items.pt: semestral; que ocorre duas vezes ao ano
items.example: The society holds a biannual conference in spring and autumn.
items.note: Bi- can express twice; for maximum clarity, say twice a year because biannual can be interpreted ambiguously.

items.example: The school is looking for bilingual teaching assistants.
items.note: Bi- means two; a bilingual person uses two languages.

items.example: He remains on good terms with his ex-wife.
items.note: Ex- means former; normally written with a hyphen before family roles.

items.example: As an ex-smoker, she understands how hard quitting can be.
items.note: Ex- means formerly; it does not mean smoking less now.

items.example: I met my ex-boss at a conference.
items.note: Ex- indicates a former role or relationship.

items.example: Scientists extract information from the recorded signals.
items.note: Here ex- means out of; extract can also be a noun with first-syllable stress.

items.example: Exhale slowly before taking another deep breath.
items.note: Ex- means out; exhale contrasts with inhale.

items.example: She specialised in microbiology during her degree.
items.note: Micro- means small, especially in relation to microscopic organisms.

items.example: A microchip stores the identification information.
items.note: Micro- means small.

items.example: The scratches were almost microscopic.
items.note: Micro- means extremely small.

items.example: Heat the leftovers in the microwave for one minute.
items.note: Micro- indicates very small wave length; common as a noun and verb.

items.example: Don't misunderstand my question; I'm asking about the design, not the deadline.
items.note: Mis- means wrongly; irregular past misunderstood.

items.example: A careless translator might mistranslate this technical term.
items.note: Mis- means badly or wrongly.

items.example: The incomplete figures could mislead investors.
items.note: Mis- means wrongly; past misled and past participle misled.

items.example: A monolingual dictionary explains words in one language.
items.note: Mono- means one, contrasted with bilingual and multilingual.

items.example: The actor delivered a moving monologue.
items.note: Mono- means one; a monologue is spoken by one person.

items.example: She works for a multinational engineering company.
items.note: Multi- means many; a multinational operates in several countries.

items.example: The presentation contains multimedia content.
items.note: Multi- means many; multimedia combines several media forms.

items.example: We bought a multipurpose tool for the workshop.
items.note: Multi- expresses multiple functions; also written multi-purpose.

items.example: Don't overdo the exercise when you are recovering from an injury.
items.note: Over- means too much; irregular past overdid and past participle overdone.

items.example: The children were overtired after the trip.
items.note: Over- means excessively.

items.pt: acordar tarde demais; dormir além da hora
items.example: I overslept and missed the early train.
items.note: Over- means more than intended; past overslept.

items.example: It's easy to overeat at a buffet.
items.note: Over- means too much; past overate, past participle overeaten.

items.example: The museum has a collection of post-war furniture.
items.note: Post- means after; often hyphenated in this adjective.

items.example: She is a postgraduate student in applied physics.
items.note: Post- means after; postgraduate study follows a first degree.

items.example: Try to set aside preconceived ideas before reading the evidence.
items.note: Pre- means before; commonly used in preconceived idea or notion.

items.example: The town still has several pre-war buildings.
items.note: Pre- means before; normally hyphenated.

items.example: Please don't prejudge the proposal before hearing the details.
items.note: Pre- means before; to prejudge is to form a judgment too early.

items.example: The editorial took a pro-government position.
items.note: Pro- means in favour of, not professional.

items.example: The article criticised several pseudoscientific claims.
items.note: Pseudo- means false or only pretending to be scientific.

items.example: He dismissed the speech as pseudo-intellectual.
items.note: Pseudo- suggests an appearance of intellectual depth without substance.

items.example: Please rewrite the introduction to make it clearer.
items.note: Re- means again; irregular past rewrote, past participle rewritten.

items.example: The company hopes to regain the trust of its customers.
items.note: Re- can mean getting something back.

items.example: We need to rearrange the chairs before the meeting.
items.note: Re- means arrange again or in a different order.

items.example: I'll repay the loan in monthly instalments.
items.note: Re- can mean back; irregular past repaid.

items.example: You need to renew your passport before it expires.
items.note: Re- can mean make new again.

items.example: The desks were arranged in a semicircular pattern.
items.note: Semi- means half; British spelling semicircular.

items.example: Our team reached the semi-final of the tournament.
items.note: Semi- means half; usually written semi-final in British English.

items.example: They moved into a semi-detached house near the station.
items.note: Semi- indicates a house joined to another on one side.

items.example: We took the subway across New York.
items.note: Sub- means under; US and UK meanings differ.

items.example: The submarine remained underwater for several weeks.
items.note: Sub- means under.

items.example: The report divides the project into several subdivisions.
items.note: Sub- indicates a smaller division within a larger whole.

items.example: The laboratory has several underused instruments.
items.note: Under- means not used as much as it could be.

items.example: The chicken was undercooked and needed more time in the oven.
items.note: Under- means insufficiently cooked.

items.example: It would be dishonest to hide the missing data.
items.note: Dis- gives honest a negative meaning.

items.example: His indiscreet remarks embarrassed his colleagues.
items.note: In- means not discreet; do not confuse discreet with discrete.

items.example: Her comment was insensitive to the family's situation.
items.note: In- negates sensitive.

items.example: The explanation sounded unconvincing to the reviewers.
items.note: Un- means not convincing.

items.example: That detail is irrelevant to the main argument.
items.note: Ir- means not; use irrelevant to something.

items.example: The child had been unusually disobedient at school.
items.note: Dis- means not obedient.

items.example: She was unemployed for several months after graduation.
items.note: Un- reverses employed; describe people, not unfilled jobs.

items.example: The old heating system is inefficient and expensive to run.
items.note: In- means not efficient.

items.example: He seemed ungrateful for all the help he had received.
items.note: Un- means not grateful.

items.example: Sharing confidential information would be disloyal to the team.
items.note: Dis- means not loyal.

items.example: The manager was intolerant of repeated delays.
items.note: In- negates tolerant; often intolerant of something.

items.example: I often mispronounce unfamiliar place names.
items.note: Mis- means wrongly; stress the second syllable of pronounce.

items.example: The staff were overworked during the holiday period.
items.note: Over- means working too much.

items.pt: mal remunerado; que recebe menos do que deveria
items.example: Many workers feel underpaid for their responsibilities.
items.note: Under- means paid too little.

items.example: The lecturer explained why the theory was pseudoscience.
items.note: Pseudo- means falsely presented as science.

items.example: We had to redo the calculation after finding an error.
items.note: Re- means do again; past redid, past participle redone.

units.title: Unit 72 — Roots
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 150–151 (PDF pages 151–152).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Recognise frequent Latin roots and use them to infer the meanings of derived English words.
Use key verbs built from DUC/DUCT, PONE/POSE, PORT, PRESS, SPECT and VERT naturally in context.
Identify person nouns and abstract nouns related to the root-based verbs.
Contrast formal Latin-based verbs with everyday two-part alternatives and recognise derived words from the exercises.

sectionsChecked: A: Verbs and a noun based on DUC/DUCT, PONE/POSE, PORT, PRESS, SPECT and VERT
B: Person and abstract nouns from Latin-root verbs

items.example: An experienced researcher will conduct the experiment tomorrow.
items.note: DUC and DUCT mean lead; conduct can mean lead an orchestra or carry out an activity.

items.example: A financial incentive might induce more people to take part.
items.note: From the root meaning lead; induce someone to do something means persuade them.

items.example: The railway crosses the valley on a stone viaduct.
items.note: Viaduct is a noun built around DUCT, meaning to lead or carry.

items.example: We may need to postpone the inspection until Friday.
items.note: PONE and POSE mean place or put; postpone means put off until later.

items.example: The general attempted to depose the country's leader.
items.note: Depose means remove someone from a position of power; a formal verb.

items.example: The authority may impose a fine for late payment.
items.note: Often impose a rule, ban, tax or restriction on someone.

items.example: She composed a short piece for the school's concert.
items.note: Compose means create or put together, especially music or written work.

items.example: I deposited the cheque in my bank account.
items.note: The verb means place something somewhere, especially money in an account.

items.example: The company will transport the equipment by rail.
items.note: PORT means carry or take; transport often refers to moving goods or people.

items.example: The factory imports electronic components from overseas.
items.note: IM- means in; import brings goods or services into a country.

items.example: Local farmers export fruit to several countries.
items.note: EX- means out; export sends goods or services abroad.

items.example: The data support the initial hypothesis.
items.note: Support can mean hold up physically or provide evidence or help; also a noun.

items.example: The authorities decided to deport the man after the legal hearing.
items.note: Deport means send a person out of a country under legal authority.

items.example: Her presentation impressed the selection committee.
items.note: Impress means cause admiration; often be impressed by something.

items.example: Grey skies can depress my mood in winter.
items.note: Depress means make someone feel unhappy; the noun depression has other uses too.

items.example: He struggled to express his concerns clearly.
items.note: Express means put thoughts or feelings into words.

items.example: Everyone must respect the laboratory's safety rules.
items.note: Respect means treat someone or something with proper regard; also a noun.

items.example: A technician will inspect the cable before installation.
items.note: Inspect means examine carefully; typically more formal than look at.

items.example: The company plans to prospect for minerals in the region.
items.note: As a verb, prospect means search for resources such as gold or minerals.

items.example: We reverted to the earlier version after the update failed.
items.note: Re- means back; commonly revert to a previous state or method.

items.example: Can you convert this file into a PDF?
items.note: Convert means change from one form to another; use convert into or to.

items.example: Roadworks diverted traffic through the village.
items.note: Divert means turn something away from its normal route or purpose.

items.example: The building inspector checked the emergency exits.
items.note: The person noun from inspect; compare inspection for the activity.

items.example: The inspection uncovered two safety problems.
items.note: An abstract noun formed from inspect with -ion.

items.example: They advertise their courses on social media.
items.note: The base verb for advertiser and advertisement.

items.example: The advertiser chose a younger target audience.
items.note: A person or company that pays for or places advertisements.

items.example: I saw an advertisement for an engineering position.
items.note: A noun for a publicity message; often shortened to advert in British English.

items.example: The lawyer met a deportee who wanted to appeal the decision.
items.note: -Ee marks the person affected by the action of deporting.

items.example: The court delayed the deportation until the appeal was heard.
items.note: The abstract noun formed from deport.

items.example: Could you introduce me to the new team member?
items.note: Introduce someone to someone; the base for introducer and introduction.

items.pt: apresentador; pessoa que faz uma introdução
items.example: The introducer briefly described the speaker's achievements.
items.note: The person noun for someone who introduces; less common than the verb.

items.example: The introduction explains the aims of the study.
items.note: A noun formed from introduce; notice the stem changes.

items.example: The authorities used the law to oppress minority groups.
items.note: Oppress means keep people under unfair, harsh control.

items.example: The novel tells the story from the viewpoint of the oppressor.
items.note: A person or group that oppresses others.

items.example: The campaign drew attention to political oppression.
items.note: An abstract noun formed from oppress.

items.example: The composer wrote music for several films.
items.note: A person who composes music; compare composition.

items.example: Her latest composition combines strings and percussion.
items.note: The work produced by composing or the act of putting things together.

items.example: The conversion from analogue to digital data is handled by this circuit.
items.note: Abstract noun from convert; notice the consonant and stress changes.

items.example: The conductor asked the orchestra to repeat the passage.
items.note: Person noun from conduct; it can also mean a material that carries electricity.

items.example: My first impression of the design was positive.
items.note: Abstract noun from impress; also means a mark or a general opinion.

items.example: She has been a supporter of the programme for years.
items.note: Person noun from support.

items.example: Compress the video before uploading it.
items.note: PRESS means push; compress means make something occupy less space.

items.example: Data compression reduced the file size significantly.
items.note: An abstract noun from compress.

items.example: The technician replaced the faulty compressor.
items.note: A machine part that compresses air or another gas; noted in the answer key.

items.example: Copper is widely used for the conduction of electricity.
items.note: From conduct; refers to the transfer of heat or electricity through material.

items.example: Her introspective essays explore memory and identity.
items.note: Intro- means inward; a person looks closely at their own thoughts and feelings.

items.example: Several residents oppose the proposed development.
items.note: O- or ob- expresses against; oppose is more formal than go against.

items.example: He tried to repress his anger during the meeting.
items.note: Re- plus PRESS; to repress a feeling is to hold it back.

items.example: We can deduce the cause from the available evidence.
items.note: DE- plus DUC; deduce means reach a conclusion through reasoning.

items.example: The investigation exposed serious weaknesses in the system.
items.note: EX- means out; here expose makes something hidden known.

items.example: She struggled to suppress a laugh during the lecture.
items.note: Sub- with PRESS suggests holding down; used for feelings, information or activity.
